## Matthew 7 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### vv. 1–2: "Do not judge, or you will be judged..."

**Traditional Reading:**
- Jesus does not prohibit all judgment. Civil courts, church discipline, and necessary private discernment are not in view. What He forbids is a **censorious, fault-finding spirit** — rashly pronouncing upon others' character, motives, or eternal state. The command targets the disposition to interpret words and deeds in the worst possible sense.
- JFB: "The thing here condemned is that disposition to look unfavorably on the character and actions of others, which leads invariably to the pronouncing of rash, unjust, and unlovely judgments upon them." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/matthew/7.htm
- Gill: It forbids "rash judgment, interpreting men's words and deeds to the worst sense, and censuring them in a very severe manner; even passing sentence on them, with respect to their eternal state and condition." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-7.html
- Spurgeon: "Use your judgment, of course… But do not indulge the criticizing faculty upon others in a censorious manner, or as if you were set in authority… This is not the day of judgment, neither are we his Majesty's judges." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-7-commentary-spurgeon
- Guzik (Enduring Word): The principle "with the measure you use, it will be measured to you" reflects a rabbinic idea that God has two measures — justice and mercy — and whichever you use on others, God uses on you. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-7/
- Calvin: "He who judges according to the word and law of the Lord, and forms his judgment by the rule of charity, always begins with subjecting himself to examination." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-7.html
- Matthew Henry: "We must not judge rashly, nor pass judgment upon our brother without any ground. We must not make the worst of people." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/matthew/7.htm

---

### vv. 3–5: The speck and the beam

**Traditional Reading:**
- The "speck" (mote/splinter) represents a small fault; the "beam" (plank/log) represents a gross, obvious sin. The humor is deliberate: a man with a plank protruding from his eye attempting delicate surgery on another's eye.
- JFB: "The 'hypocrisy' which, not without indignation, He charges it with, consists in the pretense of a zealous and compassionate charity, which cannot possibly be real in one who suffers worse faults to lie uncorrected in himself." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/matthew/7.htm
- Spurgeon: "Our reformations must begin with ourselves, or they are not true, and do not spring from a right motive… After we are ourselves sanctified, we are bound to be eyes to the blind, and correctors of unholy living; but not till then." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-7-commentary-spurgeon
- Guzik: Jesus does not forbid helping a brother with his speck — He requires that we deal with our own sin first. The point is the order of operations: self-examination before brother-correction. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-7/
- Gill notes this language was known among the rabbis: "cast out the mote out of thine eye… cast out the beam from thine eye" was a common proverbial exchange. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-7.html

---

### v. 6: Dogs, swine, and pearls

**Traditional Reading:**
- This verse balances vv. 1–5: having forbidden censorious judgment, Jesus now forbids the opposite extreme — **naïve lack of discernment**. "Dogs" and "swine" represent those who are hardened, hostile, or utterly incapable of valuing holy things.
- JFB: "Dogs — savage or snarling haters of truth and righteousness. Swine — the impure or coarse, who are incapable of appreciating the priceless jewels of Christianity." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/matthew/7.htm
- Spurgeon: "When men are evidently unable to perceive the purity of a great truth, do not set it before them… Saints are not to be simpletons; they are not to be judges, but, also, they are not to be fools." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-7-commentary-spurgeon
- Guzik sees a contextual link: the "pearl" may be godly correction offered to a brother — but when the recipient proves himself a "swine" (determined not to receive it), correction should cease. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-7/
- Gill notes the Jewish maxim: "Do not cast pearls before swine, nor deliver wisdom to him who knows not the excellency of it." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-7.html
- Ligonier connects this verse to the broader theme of discernment: while warning against judgmentalism, Jesus urges discriminating judgment — https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/discernment-thinking-gods-thoughts

---

### vv. 7–8: Ask, seek, knock

**Traditional Reading:**
- The three verbs express **increasing intensity**: asking is simple petition; seeking adds effort and pursuit; knocking adds persistence against a closed door.
- JFB: "We ask for what we wish; we seek for what we miss; we knock for that from which we feel ourselves shut out." The context suggests a link: after the difficult commands about judging and discernment, the disciples might ask, "How can we possibly do this?" Jesus answers: "Pray." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/matthew/7.htm
- Ellicott likewise sees a latent sequence: "If the work of reforming others and ourselves is so difficult, how shall we dare to enter on it? Where shall we find the courage and the wisdom which we need?" The answer: in prayer. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/matthew-7.html
- Spurgeon: "Each form of prayer is prescribed, accepted, and rewarded in a manner suitable to its character. To receive a gift is simple, to find a treasure is more enriching, to enter into a palace is best of all." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-7-commentary-spurgeon
- Guzik: God values persistence in prayer not because He is reluctant but because persistence shows we share His heart and aligns our heart with His. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-7/
- Calvin: "Nothing is better adapted to excite us to prayer than a full conviction that we shall be heard. Those who doubt can only pray in an indifferent manner." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/matthew-7.html

**Denominational Note — Word of Faith / Prosperity:**
- Some Word of Faith teachers cite "ask… seek… knock" to support "name-it-and-claim-it" theology. The traditional reading from all surveyed sources, however, qualifies the promise: Spurgeon explicitly says "It would be a terrible thing if God always gave us all we asked for" and that "our heavenly Father will correct our prayer, and give us, not what we ignorantly seek, but what we really need." JFB likewise notes that the promise presumes asking "in faith — and with an honest purpose to make use of what he receives," citing James 1:5–7 and 4:3. (I could not retrieve dedicated Word of Faith sources due to search limits, so this contrast is drawn from how the traditional commentators frame the limits.)

---

### vv. 9–11: Bread, stone; fish, serpent

**Traditional Reading:**
- Jesus uses a _qal vaḥomer_ ("how much more") argument: if even sinful human fathers give good gifts to their children, how much more will the perfectly good heavenly Father give good things.
- Spurgeon: "Our prayers go to heaven in a Revised Version… We, although ourselves evil, correct our children's blunders in their requests to us, and much more will our all-wise, and good, heavenly Father amend in his bestowals the errors of our beseechings." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-7-commentary-spurgeon
- Guzik: The "how much more" is left open-ended for meditation. God doesn't need to be persuaded or appeased; He wants to give — and gives not just what we ask but better. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-7/
- JFB notes Luke's parallel (Luke 11:13) specifies "the Holy Spirit" instead of "good things," suggesting Matthew's audience (a broader, earlier crowd) received the more general form while Luke's (disciples) received sharper doctrinal teaching. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/matthew/7.htm
- Gill: "If ye then, being evil" refers to mankind's fallen nature, not to the disciples specifically being wicked — "all mankind in general are, both by nature and practice." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-7.html

---

### v. 12: The Golden Rule

**Traditional Reading:**
- The negative form ("Do not do to others what you hate") was known in Judaism (Hillel), Greek philosophy, and Confucianism. Jesus **transforms it into the positive**: actively doing good, not merely refraining from harm.
- Guzik: "Under the negative form of the rule, the goats of Matthew 25:31-46 are found 'not guilty.' Yet under the positive form of the Golden Rule — Jesus' form — they are indeed found guilty." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-7/
- JFB calls it "the royal law," "the substance of all relative duty; all Scripture in a nutshell." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/matthew/7.htm
- Spurgeon: "This is the sum of the Decalogue, the Pentateuch, and the whole sacred Word… Oh, that all men acted on it, and there would be no slavery, no war, no swearing, no striking, no lying, no robbing; but all would be justice and love!" — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-7-commentary-spurgeon
- Gill: The "therefore" connects the Golden Rule to all that precedes. Maimonides expressed it similarly, and even the pagan emperor Alexander Severus had it inscribed on his wall. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-7.html

---

### vv. 13–14: The narrow and wide gates

**Traditional Reading:**
- Two ways, two gates, two destinations, two crowds. The narrow gate requires self-denial, repentance, and submission to Christ. The broad way requires nothing — it is the path of least resistance.
- JFB: "The first right step in religion involves a triumph over all our natural inclinations… The whole course is as difficult as the first step." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/matthew/7.htm
- Spurgeon: "Men go to ruin along the turnpike-road, but the way to heaven is a bridle-path… to be popular one must be broad — broad in doctrine, in morals, and in spirituals." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-7-commentary-spurgeon
- Gill: The "strait gate" is Christ Himself (cf. John 10:7). It is "strait" because faith in Christ, profession of it, and a life consistent with it are "attended with many afflictions, temptations, reproaches, and persecutions." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-7.html
- Guzik: Jesus "is not encouraging committed disciples, 'Christians,' to press on along the narrow way and be rewarded in the end. He is rather commanding his disciples to enter the way marked by persecution and rewarded in the end" (citing Carson). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-7/

**Denominational / Theological Note:**
- The phrase "few there be that find it" has been a traditional proof-text for particularism (only a minority are saved). The sources surveyed (Gill the Baptist, Calvin the Reformed, Spurgeon the Baptist, the Presbyterian JFB) all take this at face value. I was unable to search universalist or inclusivist readings due to tool limits.

---

### vv. 15–20: False prophets and their fruit

**Traditional Reading:**
- "Sheep's clothing" means outward appearance of piety and orthodoxy; "ravenous wolves" means inward greed, lust for power, or desire to devour the flock for selfish ends. The test is **fruit** — not merely miracles or eloquence.
- JFB: The fruit is "not their doctrines… but the **practical effect** of their teaching, which is the proper fruit of the tree." A good tree cannot produce bad fruit, and vice versa, because "the heart determines and is the only proper interpreter of the actions of our life." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/matthew/7.htm
- Spurgeon: "Their teaching, their living, and their effect upon our minds will be a sure test to us… What is the effect of modern theology upon the spirituality, the prayerfulness, the holiness of the people? Has it any good effect?" — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-7-commentary-spurgeon
- Guzik: We are to watch both the **manner of living** (righteousness, humility, faithfulness) and the **content of teaching** (is it consistent with God's Word?). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-7/
- Barclay (cited by Guzik): "The basic fault of the false prophet is self-interest" — expressed as desire for gain, an easy life, prestige, or advancing one's own ideas.

**Reformed Note:**
- The Ligonier article on discernment connects v.15 directly to v.6: discernment is necessary precisely because false prophets exist, and we must "test the spirits." — https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/discernment-thinking-gods-thoughts

---

### vv. 21–23: "Lord, Lord" — Not everyone who says

**Traditional Reading:**
- This is among the most sobering passages in Scripture. Verbal confession ("Lord, Lord" — doubled for emphasis and apparent zeal), miraculous works (prophesying, exorcism, "many wonderful works"), and even apparent success in ministry prove nothing if there is no genuine, obedient relationship with Christ.
- JFB: The reduplication "Lord, Lord" denotes zeal, yet Christ says "I never knew you" — not "I once knew you but the relationship was broken," but there **never was** a saving relationship. "They claimed intimacy with Christ, and… are represented as having gone out and in with Him on familiar terms. 'So much the worse for you,' He replies." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/matthew/7.htm
- Spurgeon: "An orthodox creed will not save if it stands alone… All the preaching in the world will not save the preacher if he does not practice… Three times over the person is described as doing all 'in thy name'; and yet the Lord, whose name he used so freely, so boldly, knew nothing of him." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-7-commentary-spurgeon
- Guzik: "It is knowing Him and being known by Him that secures salvation." The phrase "I never knew you" echoes the biblical concept of "knowing" as intimate relationship, not mere cognitive awareness. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-7/

**Key Theological Debates:**
- **Lordship Salvation controversy (Reformed/Baptist):** This passage is a central proof-text for the Lordship salvation view (associated with John MacArthur / gty.org and Reformed Baptists), which holds that saving faith necessarily produces a life of obedience, and those whose lives show only words and not deeds are not truly saved. I was unable to retrieve direct gty.org or desiringgod.org pages due to search limits.
- **Free Grace position:** Some free-grace advocates argue that these people are genuine believers who lose rewards but not salvation. The traditional reading from all surveyed sources (JFB, Spurgeon, Gill, Guzik, Calvin) uniformly treats this as a warning about false profession — those who were never truly saved. The "I never knew you" is taken as decisive.
- **Catholic and Orthodox readings:** I was unable to retrieve dedicated newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org pages within the tool limits. Typically, Catholic exegesis reads this passage in continuity with the necessity of doing the Father's will expressed through faith working through love and the sacramental life, but I could not confirm specific source citations.

---

### vv. 24–27: The two builders

**Traditional Reading:**
- Both men hear Jesus' words. Both build houses. Both face identical storms (rain from above, floods from below, winds from all sides). The sole variable is the **foundation**: rock (obedience) versus sand (hearing only).
- Spurgeon: "The hearing of the Lord's sayings sets him upon work… yet though he was industrious, he was foolish. No doubt he built quickly, for his foundation cost him no severe labor… His fundamentals were wrong." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-7-commentary-spurgeon
- JFB: The rock is "true discipleship, or genuine subjection to Christ"; sand is "an empty profession and mere external services." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/matthew/7.htm
- Guzik: "The foundation of our faith is proven only when the storms come." Jesus does not promise storm-free lives; the storms come to both builders. The question is whether the house stands through them. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-7/
- Gill: The rock represents Christ Himself, the only secure foundation (cf. 1 Corinthians 3:11). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/matthew-7.html

**Reformed / Lutheran Note:**
- JFB and Calvin would emphasize that the "doing" is evidence of genuine faith, not a meritorious work that earns salvation. The Ligonier article notes the sermon's chief purpose is "to drive us to faith in Him as the One who fulfills the law of God on behalf of His people," preventing a works-righteousness reading. — https://learn.ligonier.org/guides/the-sermon-on-the-mount

---

### vv. 28–29: The crowds were astonished at His authority

**Traditional Reading:**
- The scribes taught by quoting prior authorities ("Rabbi so-and-so said…"). Jesus taught with direct, unmediated authority: "But I say to you…" The crowds recognized the qualitative difference.
- Spurgeon closes with a searching observation: "Never was there so great a Preacher, and never did he deliver a greater discourse: how many were the penitents? How many the converts? We do not hear of any. Divine truth, even when preached to perfection, will not of itself affect the heart to conversion. The most overpowering authority produces no obedience unless the Holy Ghost subdue the hearer's heart." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-7-commentary-spurgeon
- JFB: "The consciousness of divine authority, as Lawgiver, Expounder and Judge, so beamed through His teaching, that the scribes' teaching could not but appear drivelling in such a light." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/matthew/7.htm
- Ligonier: Matthew deliberately structured the Sermon on the Mount to parallel Moses receiving the law on Sinai — presenting Jesus as the new and greater Moses. The astonishment at His authority confirms this. — https://learn.ligonier.org/guides/the-sermon-on-the-mount

### Summary of What I Could Not Retrieve

Due to tool limits (5 searches and 4 fetches reached), I was unable to search for or retrieve:
- **Catholic and Orthodox** readings from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org
- **Lutheran** (lcms.org, 1517.org) or **Methodist/Wesleyan** (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com) tradition-specific commentary
- **Modern scholarship** from bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org notes
- **Word of Faith / hyper-grace** primary sources from within those movements
- **Baptist** perspectives from desiringgod.org (Piper) or gty.org (MacArthur) — though Spurgeon (Baptist) and Gill (Baptist) are amply represented
- **Precept Austin** individual verse pages beyond what was fetched in the initial search results

The notes above are therefore strongest on the traditional evangelical/Reformed/Baptist reading (Gill, Spurgeon, JFB, Calvin, Guzik, Henry, Ellicott), which is well represented in the retrieved pages.
